JSON: Name: norway_healthworkforce_systemdynamics Title: Scenario-based system dynamics simulation to quantify the effect of combined policy interventions on projected health- and care-sector workforce demand in Norway to 2040 Short Hypothesis: A combined intervention package (raising filled-position full-time equivalent share to 90%, reallocating 20% of eligible nursing tasks to health-care assistants, and deploying digital clinician-time reductions of 15% per contact) causes a ≥30% reduction in projected net FTE demand for publicly funded health- and care-services in Norway in 2040 compared with the SSB Helsemod reference projection. Related Work: Existing work on health workforce forecasting primarily uses cohort-component and macro-level projection tools (e.g., supply-driven models and demand-driven models such as SSB's Helsemod) and scenario analyses to project FTE needs to mid-century. Other strands evaluate isolated interventions: task-shifting studies quantify time or FTE substitution potential between professions; telemedicine and digital triage studies estimate per-contact time savings and avoided visits; organizational change analyses examine effects of primary-care strengthening and integrated care on hospital use. Limitations of prior approaches include (1) strong reliance on single-intervention counterfactuals rather than joint intervention portfolios, (2) static substitution elasticities that ignore dynamic behavioral adaptations, (3) coarse regional aggregation that masks municipal heterogeneity, (4) limited calibration to observed historical productivity shocks, and (5) sparse joint evaluation of workforce, service quality (avoidable admissions), and cost outcomes under uncertainty. Abstract: This research develops an integrated scenario-based system dynamics model, combined with microsimulation of staffing allocation, to estimate the causal impact of coordinated policy interventions on Norway's health- and care-sector workforce demand through 2040. The study addresses the gap between single-intervention forecasts and system-level responses by modelling demographic drivers, care-demand flows, multi-professional task allocation, part-time/turnover dynamics, and time-savings from digital tools. We will calibrate and validate the model on historical data (2010–2019) and SSB/Helsemod outputs, then simulate policy packages: changes in full-time employment share, clinically safe task-shifting, digital clinician-time reductions, and organizational consolidation scenarios. The main contribution is quantifying marginal and joint effects of interventions on net FTE demand, service capacity metrics (avoidable admissions, wait times), and personnel costs with uncertainty quantification. Expected outcomes include ranked intervention effect sizes, sensitivity analyses, and policy-relevant thresholds for attaining sustainable workforce trajectories. Experiments: Datasets: SSB population projections (MMM), historical Helsemod inputs/outputs, SSB/municipal registers of employed health personnel by profession and FTE (2010–2021), Norwegian Patient Registry (admissions, DRG), primary-care contact registers, EHR-derived clinician time logs (where available), time-motion studies for task durations, OECD workforce indicators, and municipal-level demographic/geo data. Baselines: (A) SSB Helsemod reference scenario to 2040; (B) SSB low and high demand scenarios. Interventions modelled: I1 increase average filled-position FTE share to 0.90 (single-year phased adoption 2025–2030); I2 task-shifting: transfer 20% of eligible nursing tasks to health-care assistants with calibrated time-per-task substitution factors; I3 digital efficiency: reduce clinician time per contact by 15% via teletriage/automation; I4 organizational consolidation: simulate merged one-level service regions reducing duplication. Experimental design: build system-dynamics core for population, disease incidence/prevalence, care pathway flows, and aggregate hours-demand; embed microsimulation allocating staff to roles, shifts, overtime and turnover. Calibrate parameters on 2010–2019 data using Bayesian calibration (posterior sampling). Validation: backtest model by reproducing 2010–2019 observed FTE and service metrics; compute RMSE and coverage of 95% prediction intervals. Simulation runs: for each intervention and all pairwise and full-package combinations run 1,000 Monte Carlo draws sampling parameter uncertainty (productivity, uptake rates, migration). Outcome metrics: net required public FTE in 2040, percent reduction vs baseline, regional FTE shortfall distribution, avoidable hospitalizations per 1,000 80+ population, average wait time for specialist appointment, personnel cost changes (NOK), and quality proxy (30-day readmission). Comparisons and ablations: (1) single-intervention vs combined-package; (2) ablation removing each intervention from full package to compute marginal contribution; (3) sensitivity analyses (tornado plots) varying substitution elasticity [0.5–1.5], digital uptake [5–50%], and return rates of foreign-trained staff [50–100%]. Statistical analysis: report median and 95% credible intervals; test hypothesis threshold (≥30% reduction) using posterior distribution of percent reduction; compute partial rank correlation coefficients to identify influential parameters. Risk Factors and Limitations: Model risk: mis-specification of care pathways, incorrect substitution elasticities, and omitted behavioral feedbacks (eg. provider-induced demand) can bias effect estimates. Data risk: incomplete or non-representative clinician time logs and municipal staffing registers; inconsistent definitions of professions and FTE across sources. Validation limits: backtest covers a period with different shocks (eg. pandemic) and may not fully validate counterfactual long-term dynamics. Scalability: Bayesian calibration with microsimulation and Monte Carlo sampling may require substantial compute; results may necessitate HPC resources. Generalization: calibrated parameters are Norway-specific (demography, service mix) and findings may not transfer to countries with different provider mix or payment systems. Policy-design risk: assumed intervention uptake rates (full-time increases, task-shift adoption, digital efficacy) may not be politically or operationally feasible, so projected reductions could be optimistic. Evaluation bias: outcome proxies (avoidable admissions, readmission) imperfectly capture service quality and patient experience. Equity risk: aggregated scenarios could mask local effects and exacerbate municipal-level shortages unobserved in national aggregates.
